To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
extraintestinal pathogen E. coli (ExPEC) strains causing pneumonia have distinct phylogenetic and virulence gene profiles compared with ExPEC strains causing bacteremia and commensal E. coli.

extraintestinal pathogen E. coli pneumonia-specific isolates are characterized by a distinct virulence gene profile and antimicrobial susceptibility pattern compared with commensal and extraintestinal pathogenesis E. coli bacteremia isolates.
E. coli isolates causing pneumonia in mechanically ventilated patients have a distinct genetic and virulence profile from those of commensal and bloodstream isolates.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the genetic traits of E. coli responsible for pneumonia and with the characterization of the pathogenicity of these isolates.
the identification of the genetic and phenotypic characteristics of E. colistrains that cause pneumonia in critically ill patients.
the identification of the genetic and phenotypic characteristics of Escherichiacoli pneumonia isolates from patients receiving mechanical ventilation in France.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the pneumonia isolates are part of the extraintestinal E. coli pathogenicity group but that they have specific traits that are not found in other extraintestinal E coli isolates.
pneumonia-specific E. coli have distinct phylogenetic and virulence profiles.

E. coli pneumonia is not a disease of the elderly, but a disease of the very elderly, with a median age of 86 years, with an increasing prevalence of pneumonia in the elderly and a mortality rate of 50%.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
E. coli causing pneumonia in critically ill patients is a distinct pathovar with a specific phylogenetic and virulence profile.

the E. coli causing pneumonia in mechanically ventilated patients are not the same as the E. coli responsible for community-acquired urinary tract infections, and that they are different from the E. coli that causes bloodstream infections.
pneumonia E. coli isolates from critically patients have distinct genomic, phylogenetic, and virulence traits compared with commensal and bloodstream isolates.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the pneumonic E. coli strains are a subset of the pathogenic E. coli strains, and that they are not a new entity.
E. coli pneumonia strains are distinct from other strains of E. coli.
E. coli pneumonia in patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation is caused by a subset of extraintestinal pathogen E. coli (ExPEC) that has specific virulence and resistance profiles.
